props.title: Reform School Girls

sections.content: Reform School Girls stands as a deliciously self-aware entry in the women-in-prison exploitation genre, following the path blazed by classics like Caged (1950) but amping up the camp factor to eleven. Director Tom DeSimone deliberately pushes every genre trope to absurd extremes - the sadistic warden, brutal guards, shower scenes, and prison yard fights are all present but delivered with a knowing wink. Wendy O. Williams of the Plasmatics brings her punk sensibility as the tough inmate Charlie, while Pat Ast channels Divine in her performance as the thundering matron Edna.

sections.content: The women-in-prison genre exploded in the 1970s with Roger Corman's New World Pictures leading the charge. The Big Bird Cage (1972) and Women in Cages (1971) launched Pam Grier's career while establishing the blueprint that Reform School Girls would later satirize. These films mixed social commentary with exploitation elements, often featuring themes of institutional corruption and abuse of power beneath their sensationalistic surfaces.

Reform School Girls marked a turning point where the genre became self-referential. Like Airplane! (1980) did for disaster films, it highlighted the absurdity of its own conventions. The film's over-the-top soundtrack featuring Wendy O. Williams screaming "It's My Life" while standing atop a speeding car perfectly encapsulates its gleeful embrace of excess. movies.title: Terminal Island
movies.slug: Women and men prisoners battle for survival on an island prison colony

sections.content: While exploitation films like Reform School Girls played prison life for thrills, more serious examinations emerged in films like Brubaker (1980) and Short Eyes (1977). The women-in-prison genre's influence can be seen in later works like Orange Is the New Black (2013-2019), which similarly balances dark humor with institutional critique, though with considerably more nuance.
